rewritten_text:
I want you to form lasting connections with good society. To do that, you should have as few unsuitable friends as possible. So if you are still in this area when Mr. Martin marries, I hope your friendship with his sisters won’t lead you to make friends with his wife. She will probably be some ordinary farmer’s daughter with no education.”

“Certainly. Yes. Though I don’t think Mr. Martin would ever marry anyone who wasn’t educated and very well brought up. But I don’t mean to argue with your judgment. I’m sure I won’t want to know his wife. I shall always care a great deal for the Miss Martins, especially Elizabeth. I would be very sorry to stop seeing them, because they are just as well educated as I am. Still, if he marries an ignorant, vulgar woman, I certainly ought to avoid visiting her if possible.”

Emma watched Harriet as her opinions shifted through this speech and saw no worrying signs of love. The young man had been Harriet’s first admirer. Emma hoped that this was his only claim on her feelings, and that Harriet would not seriously resist any kindly plans Emma made for her.

They met Mr. Martin the very next day while walking along the Donwell road. He was on foot. He first looked at Emma with great respect, then at Harriet with obvious, sincere pleasure. Emma welcomed the chance to study him. She walked a few yards ahead while the others talked, and her quick eyes soon told her enough about Mr. Robert Martin. He was neatly dressed and looked sensible, but otherwise his appearance offered little to admire. She thought that, when Harriet compared him with gentlemen, she would lose all the liking she had begun to feel for him. Harriet could recognize good manners. Without being asked, she had spoken of the gentleness of Emma’s father with both admiration and surprise. Mr. Martin looked as though he did not even know what good manners were.

Their conversation lasted only a few minutes, since they must not keep Miss Woodhouse waiting. Then Harriet ran up to her, smiling and full of excitement. Miss Woodhouse hoped to settle that excitement very soon.

“Just think of meeting him by chance! How strange! He said it was only an accident that he hadn’t taken the road by Randalls. He didn’t think we ever came this way. He thought we walked toward Randalls most days.”

He did not mention Perdita, but I was sure his love for her explained his uncertain intentions. And who deserved love more than my noble-hearted sister? Who was more worthy to marry this man who would make himself king than a woman whose very glance was fit for a queen of nations? She loved him as he loved her, though disappointment had subdued her passion and ambition battled fiercely against his.

That evening we went together to the House. Raymond knew that the coming debate would discuss and decide his plans and prospects, yet he seemed cheerful and unconcerned. As we entered the coffee room, a noise like ten thousand hives of swarming bees overwhelmed us. Politicians stood in anxious groups, speaking loudly or in low, deep voices. The aristocratic party, made up of England’s wealthiest and most influential men, seemed calmer than the others, since the question would be debated without their involvement. Ryland and his supporters stood near the fire. He came from an undistinguished family but had inherited enormous wealth from his father, a manufacturer. As a young man he had witnessed the king’s abdication and the merging of the Houses of Lords and Commons. He had welcomed these gains in popular power and spent his life strengthening and extending them. Since then, landowners had become more influential. At first, Ryland had been pleased to see Lord Raymond’s schemes draw supporters away from his opponents. But matters were now going too far. The poorer nobles welcomed the prospect of a restored monarchy, expecting it to return the power and rights they had lost. The nearly dead enthusiasm for royalty was awakening again. People were ready to become willing slaves, appointing themselves subjects and bending their necks to the yoke. A few upright, courageous spirits remained to support the state. But ordinary people had grown tired of the word republic, and many longed for royalty’s glitter and display. The outcome would reveal whether they were a majority. Ryland prepared to resist. He declared that the party had grown only because he had tolerated it. Now his patience was over, and with one sweep of his arm he would clear away the cobwebs blinding his countrymen.

When Raymond entered the coffee room, his friends greeted him with something close to a shout. They gathered around, counted their supporters, and explained why they expected certain members who had not yet declared their position to join them.

“I swear,” he cried, “by the sun, by the blue sky above, and by the love burning in my heart, that if you grant my request, you will never see me again for as long as these things exist. Go home and begin your work. I will watch your progress with anxiety beyond words. Be certain that I will appear when you are ready.”

With that, he suddenly left me, perhaps afraid I might change my mind. I watched him hurry down the mountain faster than an eagle in flight. Soon he disappeared among the rises and hollows of the sea of ice.

His story had taken the entire day, and the sun was close to the horizon when he left. I knew I should hurry down to the valley before darkness surrounded me, but my heart was heavy and I walked slowly. Finding my way along the mountain’s narrow, twisting paths and keeping my footing was difficult. My mind was consumed by the emotions stirred by the day’s events. It was late at night when I reached the resting place halfway down and sat beside the fountain. Stars appeared and vanished as clouds passed over them. Dark pines stood before me, with a fallen, broken tree here and there on the ground. The scene had a profound solemnity that stirred strange thoughts in me. I cried bitterly and pressed my hands together in anguish. “Oh, stars and clouds and winds!” I cried. “You are all about to mock me. If you truly pity me, destroy my feelings and my memory. Let me become nothing. Otherwise, go away, go away, and leave me in darkness.”

These thoughts were wild and miserable. Yet I cannot explain how heavily the stars’ endless twinkling pressed upon me, or how every gust of wind sounded like a dull, dreadful sirocco approaching to burn me up.

Dawn had come by the time I reached the village of Chamounix. I did not stop to rest but went straight back to Geneva. Even within my own mind, I could find no words for what I felt. Those feelings weighed on me like a mountain, and their sheer force crushed even my anguish beneath them. In this state I returned home, entered the house, and appeared before my family. My wild, exhausted appearance frightened them deeply, but I answered none of their questions and barely spoke. I felt as though I had been cursed, as though I had no right to ask for their sympathy, as though I could never again enjoy being among them.
